paragraphs.heading: What the hotspot does
paragraphs.text: The Iceland hotspot is partly responsible for the heavy volcanic activity that formed the island of Iceland and the Iceland Plateau. Iceland ranks among the world's most active volcanic regions. Eruptions come roughly every three years on average. About a third of the basaltic lava erupted in recorded history came from Icelandic eruptions.

paragraphs.heading: Eruptions on record
paragraphs.text: Eldgjá, a fissure of Katla, erupted in 934 in what is the largest basaltic eruption ever witnessed in the world. Laki, in 1783, was the second largest. Several eruptions beneath ice caps have set off devastating glacial bursts. The most recent of these came in 2010, after Eyjafjallajökull erupted.

paragraphs.heading: Why a ridge is not enough
paragraphs.text: Iceland sits astride the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where two plates, the Eurasian and the North American, are moving apart. That is part of the reason for its intense volcanic activity, but something more is needed to explain why Iceland is a substantial island. Most of the rest of the ridge consists of seamounts, whose peaks lie below sea level. The hotspot is a region of higher temperature than the surrounding mantle, and it is also believed to hold a higher concentration of water. Water in magma lowers the melting temperature, which may also play a part in strengthening Icelandic volcanism.

paragraphs.heading: The plume idea
paragraphs.text: One explanation is the Iceland plume, a postulated upwelling of unusually hot rock in the Earth's mantle beneath Iceland. It is thought to originate deep within the mantle, possibly at the core–mantle boundary about 2,880 km down. The hotspot is thought to be the plume's expression at the surface, and the plume is believed to add to the volcanism already caused by the plates separating. The stem of the plume is believed to be narrow, perhaps 100 km across, while its head may be more than 1,000 km in diameter.

paragraphs.heading: No clear trail
paragraphs.text: Hawaii offers a contrast. There the Pacific Plate, moving over the Hawaiian hotspot, has left a clear volcanic track that progresses in time, in the Hawaiian island chain and the Emperor Seamounts. Iceland shows no such clear track. One suggested reason is that the plume sat beneath the thick Greenland craton for about 15 million years after the continents broke apart, and that its material later became entrenched in the northern Mid-Atlantic Ridge. In western Iceland there is an extinct ridge, and from it comes the theory that the plume has moved east over time.

paragraphs.heading: A long history
paragraphs.text: The earliest volcanic rocks attributed to the plume lie on both sides of the Atlantic and are between 64 and 58 million years old. This coincides with the opening of the north Atlantic, which has led to suggestions that the plume's arrival was linked to the breakup of Laurasia and perhaps contributed to it. The first plume head may have been several thousand kilometres across. Its eruptions left volcanic rocks on both sides of today's ocean basin and produced the North Atlantic Igneous Province.

paragraphs.heading: An open question
paragraphs.text: It is still under discussion whether a deep mantle plume causes the hotspot or whether it starts at a much shallower depth. Opinions differ on whether seismic studies have imaged a plume structure. Recent seismic tomography studies found anomalies in seismic wave speed under Iceland that are consistent with a hot conduit 100 km across reaching the lower mantle. On the other hand, the postulated plume shows only weakly in tomographic images of the lower mantle. That, together with geochemical evidence, has led to the theory that there is no mantle plume under Iceland at all, and that the volcanism there results from plate tectonic processes confined to the upper mantle.
